about: Two ablatives set against each other carry the whole prayer: ore, with the mouth, and pura mente, with a pure mind. The mouth has finished its work; the mind has not begun. And two more words answer each other at the close — a gift given in time, múnere temporáli, asked to become a remedy that does not end, remédium sempitérnum. After the three prayers before Communion, all of them in the singular and all of them the priest's own, this one is plural throughout: we have taken, may we receive, for us.

s02.translation: What we have taken with the mouth, O Lord, may we receive with a pure mind: and from a gift given in time may there be for us a remedy that lasts for ever.

s03.narrative: Meanwhile he holds out the chalice to the server, who pours a little wine into it, and with this he purifies himself.

w001.function: The relative with nothing to refer back to: “that which”. Latin can leave the antecedent unsaid where English needs a word for it.

w002.function: Ablative of means, and the first of the pair: what the mouth did is done, and what the mind must do has not begun. Os here is the mouth, not the bone that is spelt the same.

w003.function: Perfect, against the subjunctive that follows: the taking is finished, the receiving is still asked for.

w006.function: The second ablative of means, answering “ore” (w002).

w007.function: Cápio is the plain word for taking hold; the prayer does not ask for a second Communion but for the mind to take what the mouth already has.

w010.function: Munus is a gift with an obligation in it — the word also means a duty and a public office.

w011.function: Agrees with “múnere” (w010) and is answered by “sempitérnum” (w015) at the end of the sentence: what belongs to time is asked to become what does not.

w014.function: Subject of “fiat” (w012): may a remedy come to be. Latin puts the thing asked for last.
